messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
For fifteen years, Omar had been the paramedic you wanted to see when your world fell apart. Calm, competent, and kind, he had a steady hand and a reassuring presence that could bring order to the most chaotic scenes. That all changed seven months ago, on a rain-slicked Tuesday afternoon when the dispatcher called out an MVC on the interstate. He didn't know until he was kneeling on the wet asphalt, the smell of gasoline and antiseptic wipes filling his nostrils, that the teenager trapped in the driver's seat was his own son, Amir. He worked on him with a desperate, automatic focus, the sights and sounds of the extrication blurring into a nightmare. There are parts of that hour he simply cannot remember, blank spaces where the terror was too immense to form a coherent memory. What he does recall returns not as a thought but as a full-body experience: the specific angle of Amir’s broken arm, the cold feel of the rain, the scent of blood mixing with the sterile smell of the ambulance.

When Omar first returned to work, he believed he could push through it. Then, on a routine call for a construction worker who had fallen, the sight of the man’s compound fracture sent him reeling. In an instant, he was back on the interstate, the memory of his son’s injuries flooding him with such sensory reality that he could feel the phantom weight of the C-collar in his hands. The terror was identical, a cold wave that left him breathless and shaking. This sudden, vivid recall left him feeling intensely vulnerable, and for the rest of his shift, he was on high alert, his concentration shattered. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, choosing a seat in the breakroom that kept his back to a wall, a profound sense of threat having taken root where his confidence used to be.

This feeling of being unsafe began to bleed into every corner of his life. He had come to believe that he had failed in his most fundamental duty, not just as a paramedic but as a father. The thought, *I should have protected him*, became a constant, corrosive presence in his mind. This conviction that he had failed made the world feel treacherous, and he started interpreting every unexpected event as a potential catastrophe. His wife placing a hand on his shoulder as he stared out the window would cause him to jolt with alarm, a reaction that horrified them both. The sense of being permanently on guard made it impossible for the memories to stay buried; his hypervigilance seemed to actively seek out reminders of the accident, making it easier for the intrusive images to break through. He became convinced he couldn't rely on himself, that his instincts were broken and he was permanently damaged by what had happened.

His entire life is now organized around managing these intrusions and the overwhelming feelings they bring. The belief that he is no longer reliable has made his paramedic's uniform feel like a costume he is unworthy to wear, and he has started calling in sick, unable to face the possibility of failing another patient. The antiseptic smell of the hospital, or even seeing a news report about an accident, functions as a powerful trigger, bringing on a fresh wave of memories and a spike in his vigilance. In response to this onslaught from both his own mind and the outside world, he tries desperately to keep his thoughts at bay. He throws himself into grueling tasks around the house—demolishing a bathroom, building a deck—working until his body aches too much for his mind to race.

However, these attempts at control have only tightened the trap. The more he tries to suppress the thoughts of the accident, the more forcefully they erupt as sensory-laden flashbacks, his mind refusing to let go of the details he most wants to forget. His avoidance of work serves as daily proof of his own negative appraisal: each missed shift confirms his fear that he can't rely on himself anymore. This exhaustion and the failure of his coping strategies have only heightened his sense of being under constant threat, making him even more susceptible to triggers. Last week, his wife cut her finger while cooking, and the sight of the blood on her skin sent a jolt of pure panic through him, the memory of his son’s more grievous wounds instantly present. Omar finally sought help after his wife found him sitting in their half-finished kitchen, staring blankly at the wall, unable to account for the last two hours. He is terrified that the calm, capable man he once was is gone for good, but a small part of him hopes that therapy might help him find a way to live with the ghosts of that rainy Tuesday, and to once again be the husband and father his family deserves.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that encountering triggers directly leads Omar to engage in maladaptive coping strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not describe how Omar's negative beliefs about himself or the world make him more susceptible to triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain how the intrusive trauma memory leads to or reinforces Omar's negative appraisals of himself.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that experiencing the trauma memory makes Omar more sensitive or hyper-aware of external triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not describe how Omar's general sense of threat or hypervigilance causes the intrusive trauma memories to occur.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain that Omar's feeling of being under threat causes or strengthens his negative beliefs about himself.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not state that Omar's use of maladaptive strategies makes him more sensitive or reactive to triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The terror was identical, a cold wave that left him breathless and shaking.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time an image from that day broke through with such force, it served as visceral proof for the thought that followed: a competent paramedic, a good father, would not be falling apart like this. It felt like a confirmation of his own profound failure.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, choosing a seat in the breakroom that kept his back to a wall, a profound sense of threat having taken root where his confidence used to be.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling so profoundly unsafe, even in the familiar setting of his own station, was the most convincing proof he had that something inside him had broken beyond repair. This persistent feeling of danger also seemed to keep his mind primed for the worst, and on days when his vigilance was highest, the memories of the accident were hardest to keep at bay, as if his brain was rehearsing the trauma to prepare for the next one.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The belief that he is no longer reliable has made his paramedic's uniform feel like a costume he is unworthy to wear, and he has started calling in sick, unable to face the possibility of failing another patient.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His avoidance of the hospital has ironically made it a more powerful trigger; now, even driving past the building or seeing a picture of an ambulance can feel like a direct confrontation with his perceived failure.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What he does recall returns not as a thought but as a full-body experience: the specific angle of Amir’s broken arm, the cold feel of the rain, the scent of blood mixing with the sterile smell of the ambulance.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because these fragments returned with such sensory intensity, he began to see echoes of them everywhere; the smell from a first-aid kit or the sight of rain on a car windscreen could now bring the entire memory rushing back.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The antiseptic smell of the hospital, or even seeing a news report about an accident, functions as a powerful trigger, bringing on a fresh wave of memories and a spike in his vigilance.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
It is on days when he encounters one of these reminders that he is most likely to call in sick, or to start a new, physically punishing project at home, a desperate attempt to outrun the internal chaos the trigger has unleashed.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He became convinced he couldn't rely on himself, that his instincts were broken and he was permanently damaged by what had happened.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This conviction that he was fundamentally compromised meant that things he would have once dismissed—a distant siren, a car backfiring—now snagged his attention, each one feeling like a potential sign of another disaster he would be helpless to prevent.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The sense of being permanently on guard made it impossible for the memories to stay buried; his hypervigilance seemed to actively seek out reminders of the accident, making it easier for the intrusive images to break through.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This constant state of threat served only to reinforce his belief that he was broken, as he felt that a normal person, a capable person, would not be living with this level of fear.
<<<END>>>
